title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
summary:
arXiv:2611.31608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.

event_model_payload.title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension

title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
summary:
arXiv:2611.31687v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

event_model_payload.title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization

title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification
summary:
arXiv:2611.31898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose an e-process stopping rule in the best-arm identification problem. The e-process stopping rule is different from the Chernoff stopping rule by its hypothesis structure on the stopping decision. The major benefit of an e-process stopping rule is the flexibility in stopping rule design and in fact, it recovers previously suggested Chernoff stopping rule on several bandit problems. Moreover, we analyze the asymptotic optimality of the $\delta$-PAC algorithm with the decomposition of e-processes. The decomposition separates optimality conditions into three parts; the sampling policy allocation convergence, the efficiency of e-process design, and the bandit problem's inherent stochastic behavior. Subsequently, we prove a sufficient condition for asymptotic optimality in bandit algorithms. For the application of an e-process stopping rule, we derived an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the generalized linear bandit problem.

event_model_payload.title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification

title: DUST: Directional Uncertainty-aware and Scale-invariant Transfer Learning
summary:
arXiv:2611.31948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transfer learning seeks to improve efficiency in a target regression task by borrowing information from related external source dataset(s). Existing approaches achieve this by enforcing Euclidean proximity between the target and source regression parameters or, more recently, by encouraging their directional alignment through angle-based penalties. While such angle-based penalties mitigate the sensitivity of the transfer learning methods to the scale differences between source and target regression coefficients, they still rely on a point estimate of the source regression parameter and thus provide no direct mechanism to incorporate uncertainty in the source information. To that end, we propose a probabilistic framework for transfer learning that operates at the level of a \emph{scale-invariant directional distribution} of the source regression parameter estimate, rather than its point estimate, to enable robust, scale-invariant and uncertainty aware transfer under heterogeneous source information. Specifically, we project the sampling distribution of the source regression estimate onto the unit sphere, thereby extracting its scale-free directional distribution. Transfer from source to target is then induced through a novel \emph{angular cone prior} which shrinks the target regression parameter towards directions in which the source distribution assigns high probability, while allowing its magnitude to be learned exclusively from the target dataset. The proposed construction admits exact finite-sample characterizations of posterior angular concentration and posterior computation remains tractable via careful low-dimensional augmentation in the parameter space.

event_model_payload.title: DUST: Directional Uncertainty-aware and Scale-invariant Transfer Learning

title: A Minimax Optimal Leave One Out Bound for Bounded Losses
summary:
arXiv:2611.31972v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study proper leave-one-out prediction with $M$ real-valued experts on $n$ fixed inputs. Each label is hidden in turn, and the learner uses the remaining labels to choose one of the experts' predictions at the held-out input. We determine how closely such a rule can match the average loss of the best single expert on the full sample. For any bounded loss that is a continuous nondecreasing function of absolute error and vanishes at zero, let $B$ denote its maximum value. Over classes of size $M$ and samples on which the best expert has average loss at most $r$, the minimax excess loss is of order $\min\{B, \sqrt{\frac{Br\log M}{n}}+\frac{B\log M}{n}\}$. For each class and loss, one deterministic rule attains this rate for every $r\in[0,B]$. The matching lower bound holds even for randomized proper rules given $r$.

event_model_payload.title: A Minimax Optimal Leave One Out Bound for Bounded Losses

title: EnSurv: Deep Generative Survival Modeling with Application to Kidney Graft Outcomes
summary:
arXiv:2611.32127v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment for life-threatening end-stage renal disease, providing significant survival advantages over dialysis. Given the severe shortage of donor organs, accurately predicting the time to premature graft failure is an essential clinical task for optimizing organ allocation and tailoring individualized immunosuppressive therapies. This study is motivated by a comprehensive United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) dataset containing 243,443 kidney transplant records with complex multi-region structures and high right-censoring rates. We propose EnSurv (survival engression), a deep generative survival framework designed to capture complex, non-linear clinical covariate interactions for modeling time to graft failure. Within a pre-additive noise model (pre-ANM) family, EnSurv optimizes an energy score augmented with pooled Kaplan-Meier tail completion to handle right-censoring. We identify the pooled-completion target of the objective, establish consistency for its best approximation within the pre-ANM family, and give conditions and error bounds for its relation to true conditional graft survival. EnSurv also provides global explainability through summaries of fitted feature weights and incorporates domain constraints through established clinical directions using a soft gradient penalty. Extensive simulation experiments were conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method in comparison with existing methods. Application to the UNOS cohort demonstrates that EnSurv effectively models individual and region-level effects, consistently outperforming baselines across evaluation metrics encompassing discrimination, calibration, and accuracy.

event_model_payload.title: EnSurv: Deep Generative Survival Modeling with Application to Kidney Graft Outcomes

title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
summary:
arXiv:2611.32391v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.

event_model_payload.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories

title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
summary:
arXiv:2611.32945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.

event_model_payload.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation

title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
summary:
arXiv:2611.32947v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.

event_model_payload.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data

title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration
summary:
arXiv:2611.31245v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: TabPFN has already shown useful predictive performance on near-infrared spectra. RamanPFN subsequently proposed two spectral representations for tabular inference: Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE). We assess whether these representations also help on datasets assembled through the nirs4all ecosystem, and whether their value extends to classical calibration. We reanalyse completed experiments from a public spectral dataset catalogue. On a post-hoc subset of 61 matched numerical prediction tasks, after excluding ten class-code, metadata or semantically ambiguous targets, LVSE reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum TabPFN by 10.22%, 12.80% and 14.52% on average for checkpoints 2.5, 3 and 3.5, respectively, with median reductions of 4.99%, 4.74% and 7.82%. Across 76 classification datasets, weighted F1 increases by 2.22, 2.56 and 3.81 percentage points. The 2.5 classification procedure uses output coding on 15 datasets exceeding the checkpoint's native class limit. GCU alone is less reliable in this implementation. LVSE also improves PLS and Ridge in many cases, with median RMSE reductions of 4.75% and 1.89%. Adding LVSE candidates to an operator-adaptive model is feasible, but a separate 35-task panel derived from the public AOM benchmark shows only small median gains. These results motivate evaluating LVSE alongside existing representation choices. They do not establish that a selector choosing between raw and LVSE inputs will improve every task.

event_model_payload.title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration

title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space
summary:
arXiv:2611.31439v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query.
  Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.

event_model_payload.title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space

title: SOTS: Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection
summary:
arXiv:2611.31525v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Training data selection for machine learning models is a critical bottleneck in industrial applications where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing coreset selection methods for time series either ignore temporal structure entirely or cannot handle variable-length, irregularly sampled, multi-channel signals, the setting most common in industrial monitoring and testing. We introduce SOTS (Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection), an unsupervised coreset selection framework for irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) classification. Each sample is mapped to a truncated path signature, capturing the joint geometric structure of its channels, and the coreset is selected by greedily minimizing the Sliced Wasserstein distance between the empirical signature distributions of the candidate subset and the full dataset, a criterion for which we establish a convergence guarantee for random coresets. We validate SOTS on a real-world, highly imbalanced industrial I&C testing dataset, where SOTS-Greedy exceeds 95% of full-dataset accuracy using only 30% of the training data, outperforming standard coreset baselines at most budgets. This advantage generalizes to public UEA regular multivariate time series benchmarks specifically when class-discriminative information is purely geometric.

event_model_payload.title: SOTS: Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection

title: Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling
summary:
arXiv:2611.31526v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural operator uncertainty quantification approaches often characterize predictive uncertainty without separately identifying the contributions of individual sources of epistemic uncertainty. Finite sampling of the training function space, output discretization, and model initialization can produce substantial variation among learned operators even when the underlying physical problem is deterministic. We systematically investigate these sources of epistemic uncertainty across a diverse set of operator learning architectures. Across our experiments, we train approximately 46,000 neural operator models and construct ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to characterize distributions of relative $L_2$ error rather than individual trained realizations. We find substantial architecture-dependent differences in epistemic uncertainty, with model initialization often accounting for the largest proportion of variance in relative $L_2$ error. The ranked performance of neural operator architectures can invert as the number and spatial distribution of output samples change, with the best architectures under sparse or randomly sampled observations differing from those at higher-resolution or structured discretizations. Furthermore, ensembles that reliably characterize aggregate operator error can provide unreliable estimates of error quantiles for individual test functions. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing the sources of epistemic uncertainty when evaluating neural operator reliability and establishing robust benchmarking practices.

event_model_payload.title: Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling

title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference
summary:
arXiv:2611.31540v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.

event_model_payload.title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference

title: Bayesian Data Integration and Model Updating in Probabilistic Digital Twins
summary:
arXiv:2611.31620v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This paper proposes a framework for sequential Bayesian updating in probabilistic digital twins using data from multiple sources collected over time. The framework distinguishes between property data and behavior data, according to how observations relate to the digital state. Property data directly inform a subset of the uncertain model parameters and can therefore be incorporated using efficient dedicated Bayesian updating methods. Behavior data provide indirect information through the prediction model and require the solution of a Bayesian inverse problem. To reduce the associated computational cost, an active-learning-based surrogate strategy is introduced that evolves with the digital state and adaptively refines the prediction model in regions relevant to posterior inference. The framework is evaluated using an idealized cantilever beam example and a geotechnical case study of a canal wall subject to varying water levels and corrosion. The examples show how complementary data sources, including both equality observations and inequality information from observed system survival, can inform uncertain parameters and system reliability. The proposed surrogate-based updating scheme yields posterior estimates and prediction accuracy comparable to those of physics-based updating while requiring substantially fewer model evaluations. The proposed framework thus supports multi-source updating and reliability assessment in probabilistic digital twins of engineering systems.

event_model_payload.title: Bayesian Data Integration and Model Updating in Probabilistic Digital Twins

title: A Kernel Framework for Linear Operator Equations
summary:
arXiv:2611.31626v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Differential, boundary, and integral operators are represented by their Riesz representers in the RKHS. The equations are solved in the regularized least-squares sense at finitely many collocation points. The solution is a finite linear combination of operator-induced representers and is obtained from a single linear system. Its sensitivities, such as financial Greeks, follow by direct differentiation. To reduce the computational cost for large collocation sets, we introduce a Nystr\"om approximation based on subsampling the operator-induced representers. It yields the best approximation of this solution within the reduced trial space, in a regularized empirical norm. Numerical examples cover ordinary, partial, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing.

event_model_payload.title: A Kernel Framework for Linear Operator Equations

title: Generating health variables for a synthetic population of Santa Catarina, Brazil, via ensemble learning and a calibrated linear program
summary:
arXiv:2611.31726v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Agent-based models in epidemiology require synthetic populations with health-related attributes, which in Brazil are available only from sample surveys such as the Pesquisa Nacional de Sa\'ude (PNS). We add health variables, including smoking, alcohol consumption, physical exercise, self-rated health and chronic conditions, to a georeferenced synthetic population of the state of Santa Catarina. Class probabilities are estimated by an ensemble of logistic regression, random forest and support vector machine, and individuals are assigned to classes by a linear program that reproduces the class proportions estimated from the survey. We show that, under a mild condition satisfied by our ensemble, the penalty term of this program is no longer needed, and the proportions are reproduced exactly. In a cross-validation on PNS data, the method attains the best results.

title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
summary:
arXiv:2611.31914v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.

title: The Generalized Volterra Signature
summary:
arXiv:2611.31967v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we introduce the generalized Volterra signature \(\gvsig(\bX)\) of a path \(\bX\), extending the classical Volterra signature introduced in [Hager, Harang, Pelizzari \& Tindel, arXiv:2603.04525, 2026], which extends Lyons' path signature to the Volterra setting. We establish a new algebraic structure to encode the generalized Volterra signature. We also establish a generalized Chen's identity. By restricting the differential trees to ladder trees, we introduce the geometric Volterra signature \(\geovsig(\bX)\) and establish the shuffle product of its signature components. To the best of our knowledge, the shuffle product for the Volterra signature is the first of its kind and allows us to formulate a universal approximation theorem for geometric Volterra signatures. For a special class of kernel functions, we prove the existence of an extended path \(\Bar{\bX}\) and relate its classical signature to the geometric Volterra signature of the original path \(\bX\).

title: Metric-Dependent Scaling Laws for Sketched Multiclass Softmax Regression
summary:
arXiv:2611.31995v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study scaling laws for full-batch gradient descent with general stable deterministic learning rates in sketched multiclass softmax regression. In a Gaussian teacher student model with power law feature and teacher spectra, the student observes a random feature sketch and reuses a finite labeled sample throughout optimization. Sketching generally makes the student misspecified, so the analysis must jointly account for approximation, nonlinear finite time learning, and the fixed empirical perturbation induced by data reuse. On an exponentially likely sketch event, we show that cross entropy excess and excess zero one risk share a common spectral scale, consisting of a resolution term and an effective learned dimension divided by sample size; teacher student decision disagreement follows the square root of that scale. The resulting balance gives rate optimal sketch and cumulative horizon choices, and synthetic experiments support the predicted regimes and metric dependent exponents.

title: Seldon TFM family: Seldon-Mini, Seldon and Seldon+
summary:
arXiv:2611.32257v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce Seldon, a family of tabular foundation models. Our classifier Seldon+ ranks first among 15 models on TabBench, our benchmark of 124 classification datasets, and on its variant with missing values. In our own runs of public benchmarks, it also ranks first on BeyondArena IID classification and TabBench-Bio, and second on TabArena classification. The open-weight models Seldon-Mini (27M parameters) and Seldon (213M parameters) both lie on the TabArena Pareto front of Elo against inference time: no entry is both more accurate and faster. On TabArena, Seldon ranks fourth and Seldon-Mini seventh among 109 leaderboard entries, and on the IID track of BeyondArena, Seldon ranks second among 42 entries. Seldon-Mini and Seldon handle both classification and regression, use an architecture similar to those of Kumo-Tabular, TabFM and TabPFN-3.5, and are trained on synthetic tables only.

title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
summary:
arXiv:2611.32372v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

event_model_payload.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling

title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
summary:
arXiv:2611.32762v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.

event_model_payload.title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates

title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
summary:
arXiv:2611.33036v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.

event_model_payload.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems

title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
summary:
arXiv:2611.33064v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.

event_model_payload.title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning

title: Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure
summary:
arXiv:2507.19423v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The paper studies a multilayer network on the same collection of nodes, where each layer follows the Generalized Random Dot Product Graph Model. Furthermore, all layers can be partitioned into groups, each group with its own unique latent subspace structure, but otherwise the matrices of connection probabilities can all be different. This setting is extremely general and includes most multilayer network models as special cases. In addition, we are interested in the situation where the layer networks may be extremely sparse and, therefore, the layer-by-layer analysis is unreliable. This problem can also be seen as a generalization of the classic setting in which one recovers a shared structure across an entire collection of matrices, extending it to the case where such structures are shared only within specific groups of matrices. The key task in this setting is to recover the groups of layers with unique subspace structures, since, after that, the information in those groups of layers can be pooled together by well-studied methods. Until now, clustering of layers in such networks was based on layer-by-layer analysis, which required the multilayer network to be sufficiently dense. Our paper is the first to provide a tensor-based approach to the problem that combines information from all layers in an unconventional manner. Our theoretical results, established under intuitive and non-restrictive assumptions, assert that the new technique achieves perfect clustering under sparsity conditions that, up to logarithmic factors, coincide with the computational lower bound derived for a much simpler model. The paper also delivers a nuanced message about the applicability of the new technique.

title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry
summary:
arXiv:2511.01064v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Variational inference (VI) approximates a target density $p$ by the best match $q$ in a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable distributions. The variational approximation is found by minimizing a divergence, most commonly the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence $\text{KL}(q||p)$, although other divergences can be considered. In practice, $p \notin \mathcal Q$ and so the optimal variational approximation is misspecified. Despite this misspecification, it was recently shown that the minimizer of $\text{KL}(q||p)$ is guaranteed to recover the mean in the presence of even symmetry and likewise the correlation matrix in the presence of elliptical symmetry for a log-concave target $p$. We extend this result in several directions. First, we relax the assumption of log-concavity and instead merely require $p$ to be unimodal, allowing for heavy-tailed targets. Second, we obtain guarantees for cases where $p$ exhibits symmetry along some but not all of its coordinates. These partial symmetries arise naturally in Bayesian hierarchical models, where the prior induces a challenging geometry but still possesses axes of symmetry. Third, we extend these guarantees to $f$-divergences, a broad class which includes the forward and reverse-KL divergences and the $\alpha$-divergences.

event_model_payload.title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry

title: Jacobian-Velocity Bounds for Deployment Risk Under Covariate Drift
summary:
arXiv:2605.04932v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study long-horizon deployment of a frozen predictor under dynamic covariate shift. A time-domain Poincar\'e inequality first reduces temporal risk volatility to derivative energy, and a Jacobian-velocity theorem supplies the corresponding pathwise control. A remainder extension separates the model-mediated, controllable term from conditional-risk variation not transmitted through the score Jacobian. Under low-rank drift, the bound decomposes the controllable term into tangent energy parallel and orthogonal to the drift subspace. This motivates drift-aligned tangent regularization (DTR), its anisotropic extension with a weaker orthogonal guardrail, and a matched monitoring proxy. Controlled experiments verify the temporal inequality, the efficiency of directional smoothing, and the necessity of the remainder term. The main field study uses a 128-dimensional gas-sensor array over ten chronological batches. A rank-4 basis estimated entirely before deployment beats ten matched random subspaces, and validation-selected anisotropic DTR improves deployment cross-entropy and volatility over pure DTR in all ten matched seeds while retaining substantially more accuracy than isotropic smoothing. Air Quality and power-consumption studies provide complementary regression evidence. Together, the results support a precise design rule: concentrate smoothness along expected motion, and use limited orthogonal smoothing when the estimated drift subspace may be incomplete.

title: A Unified Heat-Ball Framework for Fokker--Planck Equations: Mean-Value Identities, Exact Sampling, and Error Analysis
summary:
arXiv:2606.27954v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion-based generative models with nonlinear or learned forward drifts raise questions that stay hidden for Gaussian forward processes: how the divergence-free and gradient parts of the drift shape the evolving density, whether sampling can draw on local rather than global information, and how to treat low-density regions, where $u$ carries a weak signal while $\log u$ diverges and the entropy density $u\log u$ falls between the two. These questions motivate the present study of local representations for Fokker--Planck equations with general, possibly nonlinear and time-dependent drift. We derive inhomogeneous heat-ball identities for the density $u$, the log-density $\log u$, the entropy density $u\log u$, and the score $\nabla\log u$, keeping the source terms generated by the drift; their unscaled residuals recover the corresponding differential residuals at leading order in the squared heat-ball radius. The weights appearing in the identities, the source integrals, and the integration-by-parts formulas all belong to a single Beta--Gamma family of measures on the heat ball, which gives exact rejection-free sampling, product quadrature, and unbiased Monte Carlo estimators with variance and cost bounds that are explicit in the dimension and the radius. Experiments with Gaussian-mixture and nonlinear-drift references, in dimensions up to $1024$ where applicable, confirm the sampling laws, the identities, and the residual behavior. In particular, log-density and score evaluations remain accurate where direct density estimation breaks down, and the heat-ball residuals provide local consistency tests for learned score models. A study of gauge-based heat-ball walks illustrates a recursive use of the density identity.

title: qshap: Fast Shapley Decomposition of $R^2$ for Gradient-Boosted Trees
summary:
arXiv:2608.24104v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Numerous methods have been developed to quantify feature attributions in individual predictions for tree ensembles. However, many applications require global measures of feature contributions to overall model performance. Although local attribution scores can be aggregated to characterize feature importance, such summaries do not directly decompose measures of predictive performance, such as $R^2$. This article introduces qshap, available in both R and Python, which provides Shapley decomposition of $R^2$ values for gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) to quantify feature-specific contributions to model performance. By decomposing the quadratic loss of individual observations, qshap provides flexible tools to explore the importance of individual features and observations. qshap currently supports widely used GBDT implementations, including xgboost, lightgbm, and catboost, through a unified tree representation and efficient C++ backends. Its modular design can accommodate other GBDT implementations built from binary decision trees. In addition, we introduce a specialized backend for oblivious trees that exploits their symmetric structure to substantially accelerate computation.
